unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder page for Salvia elegans (taxonid=292043) fails TLS certificate verification for non-browser clients but renders in a browser. Its structured rows read 'Common Name: pineapple sage', 'Height: 3.00 to 4.00 feet', 'Spread: 2.00 to 3.00 feet', 'Sun: Full sun', 'Water: Medium' and 'Attracts: Hummingbirds, Butterflies'. toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail are null: NC State's page for Salvia elegans has no poison section and no admissible source reached names this species as toxic or safe for cats or dogs.

is_edible is true from NC State's Edibility field (teas, potpourri, cream cheese, jams, jellies) and its description of edible flowers. Neither this page nor the RHS page gives preparation times, conditions or a poison-part list.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant. NC State's Plant Type field lists Annual, Edible, Herb and Herbaceous Perennial, it gives USDA zones 8a-10b and Landscape Themes for in-ground gardens, and it says the plant dies down with the first frost and grows back in mild climates. RHS lists it as a tender perennial for conservatory or greenhouse, and its 'Under glass' cultivation run is genus-style boilerplate, so it was not used as houseplant evidence.
soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null: NC State gives 'Neutral (6.0-8.0)' only, and RHS lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral', so no floor or ceiling can be set.

water_regime is null: NC State says 'moist, well-drained soil' and that leaves drop with insufficient moisture, which are a soil adjective and a drought-stress remark rather than a watering instruction. No source reached gives a watering statement.
soil_drainage 'moderate' comes from NC State's Soil Drainage tags (Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry) and its prose 'moist, well-drained soil'. RHS says only 'Well-drained'.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only. NC State's structured Light field lists 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', but its prose says 'Pineapple sage will grow best in full sun in moist, well-drained soil.' and its tag reads '#partial shade tolerant'. RHS's Position field lists Full sun only. Missouri Botanical Garden's structured row reads 'Sun: Full sun', and its prose says 'Tolerates light shade, poor soils and some drought.' (MoBot read in a browser by the auditor; not cited, see the MoBot entry). part_shade is therefore not landed. direct_sun_hours_max is null because the only hour figures are in NC State's site-wide light legend.

Size disagreement: NC State gives 3-5 ft high and 3-4 ft wide (36-60 in and 36-48 in), used here, and its description says it 'grows 3 to 5 feet high and 3 to 4 feet wide'. RHS gives Max Height 0.5-1 metres (19.7-39.4 in) and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres (3.9-19.7 in), and its description says 'to 1m tall'. Missouri Botanical Garden gives 'Height: 3.00 to 4.00 feet' and 'Spread: 2.00 to 3.00 feet' (36-48 in and 24-36 in; read in a browser by the auditor, not cited).

No admissible source reached states a temperature range, a chill-damage onset figure, humidity, light in foot-candles or a fertilizing schedule. NC State only says the plant dies down to the ground with the first frost, which is not a damage-onset temperature.

records.name_note: NC State is the only admissible source with a dedicated Capsicum frutescens page that loaded (the RHS URLs tried returned 404, Clemson returned 403). Its page-title parenthetical reads "Bird Pepper, Capsicum, Hot Pepper, Tabasco Pepper" and its rendered Common Name(s) list stacks the same four names in the same alphabetical order. Tabasco Pepper is chosen as common_name because the page's Description uses it as the plant's name ("Tabasco Pepper is a multi-branched erect annual or perennial plant...") and lists Capsicum, Bird Pepper and Hot Pepper as "other common names". NC State also lists Capsicum conoides and Capsicum minimum under "Previously known as:". No content was borrowed from the C. annuum or C. chinense pages; this catalog already carries Capsicum annuum as Pepper and Capsicum chinense as Habanero Pepper.
records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Plant Toolbox page for Capsicum frutescens. The page has no Poison block, so there is no severity rating or poison-part list to report. Its Problems field under Landscape reads "Problem for Children". The page carries no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag. Tags as rendered: #edible fruits #red fruits #shrub #white flowers #green leaves #herbaceous perennial #contact dermatitis #perennial #edible garden. Plant Type values as rendered: Annual, Edible, Herbaceous Perennial, Vegetable, Warm Season Vegetable. Edibility is conditional. The Description says: "Most plants of the Solanaceae family contain poisonous alkaloids." and "Only the fruits of this plant should be ingested." The Edibility field says: "The Tabasco Pepper fruit may be served raw or cooked and is normally very hot when used as a flavoring. It may also be dried and ground into a powder for flavoring. Only the fruits of this plant should be ingested." Handling warning: "The sap of the plant can cause the skin to blister. It is important to wear gloves when handling this plant." The page also says "Gloves and garden shears are recommended when harvesting the peppers." and that the fruits contain 0.1-1.5 % capsaicin. The page states no capsaicin warning about eyes. The only skin warning is the sap and glove statement above. No admissible source scopes toxicity to cats or dogs, and the page's Wildlife Value text about birds is not a pet-toxicity statement.
unknowns: Only one admissible source (NC State) has a dedicated page for Capsicum frutescens that could be read. RHS capsicum-frutescens URLs returned 404 and Clemson HGIC returned 403. No MoBot, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA page for this exact species was found, so every non-null value rests on the NC State page alone.

toxic_to_pets is null. NC State's only toxicity statements are the unscoped Solanaceae alkaloid sentence, 'Problem for Children', and the sap skin-blistering and contact dermatitis notes. None names cats or dogs, and the page has no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag.

is_edible is true with a condition. Only the fruits are to be ingested, and other plant parts are not covered by the edibility statement. Most Solanaceae contain poisonous alkaloids per the page. No capsaicin eye-contact warning appears on the page. The only handling warning is the sap skin-blistering and glove statement.

soil_drainage is moderate. NC State's structured field says only 'Good Drainage'. The reading is supported by the prose pairing 'well-drained' soil with 'consistent moisture levels'. It is not fast, because the page does not describe sharp or sandy drainage as a requirement (sand is just one of four listed soil textures).

water_regime keep_moist rests on one prose sentence ('not drought tolerant and need consistent moisture levels'). The page's Resistance To Challenges field lists Drought as a tag, which conflicts with that sentence. The page gives no watering interval, so the day-interval and dry-down fields are null.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field lists 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)'. Partial Shade is mapped to part_shade. direct_sun_hours_max is null, because the only hour figures are inside NC State's generic light-category legend.

chill_damage_f is null. The page says plants 'should be brought indoors if temperatures are predicted to drop below 28 degrees Fahrenheit'. That is a bring-indoors threshold, not a stated damage-onset temperature. USDA zones 9a-11b are a hardiness rating, not an onset figure.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null. NC State's Soil pH tags are Acid (<6.0), Alkaline (>8.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0). The open-ended bands give no ceiling or floor, and the prose says only 'prefer an acidic pH, but they will tolerate neutral and alkaline soils'.

soil_base is null. The page names no container mix or bed type beyond 'humus-rich, well-drained loam, or light sandy soils', and its Landscape Location is Container with Landscape Theme Edible Garden.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant. NC State's Plant Type field lists Annual, Edible, Herbaceous Perennial, Vegetable and Warm Season Vegetable, with no Houseplant value, and its Landscape Location is Container only. The page's 'Plants should be brought indoors if temperatures are predicted to drop below 28 degrees Fahrenheit.' is cold protection for an outdoor plant, not indoor culture.

attracts_pollinators is null. NC State's Attracts field lists only Songbirds, and its Wildlife Value text is about birds. The prose 'The plant is pollinated by insects' does not say the plant attracts pollinators.

Mature size comes from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 4 ft. 0 in. - 6 ft. 0 in. = 48-72 in; Width 1 ft. 6 in. - 2 ft. 0 in. = 18-24 in). The Description gives the same 4-6 feet tall and 1.5 to 2 feet wide.
Humidity, temperature ranges, light in foot-candles and fertilizer values are not stated on any readable admissible page for this species, so they are null.

records.name_note: NC State's dedicated Cichorium endivia page has the bare binomial as its H1. Its rendered Common Name(s) list is Batavia, Endive, Escarole, Frisée, alphabetized and in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, so Batavia is first and Endive second. The description text calls the plant endive. The page says it may be confused with chicory, Belgian endive or radicchio, which it calls a different species of the same genus, and its sidebar names Cichorium intybus as the often-confused plant; that species is not covered by this record. Only NC State was used; no second source with a dedicated page was retrieved. common_name is Endive, the second listed name, because NC State's description prose opens with it ('Endives are an important bitter-tasting salad green in Europe but less well known in this country.') and uses it throughout; neither Batavia nor Endive is an already-landed common_name in this catalog.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's "Poisonous to Humans" block is human-scoped, not a cat or dog rating: Poison Severity Low (the page header also says low severity poison characteristics); Poison Symptoms: Skin irritation after exposure to sap; Poison Toxic Principle: Lactucin and lactucopicrin; Poison Part: Sap/Juice; Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. The same page nevertheless lists "Contact Dermatitis" under Problems and carries a #contact dermatitis tag, which sits oddly beside the block's "No". No Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag appears on the page. Tags carried with it: #spring greens, #cool season vegetable, #edible garden, #blue flowers, #full sun tolerant, #contact dermatitis, #edible flowers, #edible leaves, #fast growing, #microgreens; Plant Type: Annual, Cool Season Vegetable, Edible, Vegetable. Edibility (NC State): "Leaves are edible raw or cooked." and "Blue flowers are used raw in a salad, as a garnish or pickled." No handling warning or preparation times are given.

No record already in this catalog uses Mexican Marigold as its common_name, but the string appears as an alias elsewhere: NC State's Common Name(s) list for Tagetes erecta (landed as African Marigold) includes Mexican Marigold, and RHS lists Mexican marigold among the other names of Tithonia rotundifolia (landed as Mexican Sunflower). records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Plant Toolbox, Tagetes lucida page. Its block is headed "Poisonous to Humans", so everything below is human-scoped. The page carries no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tags. Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms: "Skin redness, burning pain, and blisters when broken skin is in contact with cell sap plus sunlight; nose and eye irritation from aroma of flowers." Poison Toxic Principle: Phototoxic thiophene derivatives. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Flowers, Leaves, Roots. Plant Type tags on the same page: Annual, Herb, Herbaceous Perennial. Handling warning from the Description: "The juice, sap, or thorns of these plants may cause a painful skin rash or irritation. Wash the affected area of skin with soap and water as soon as possible after contact." The Description also says the plant is often used in tea, to color foods, and as a substitute for tarragon, "however, it can be harmful if eaten in large amounts." The Edibility field says: "Flowers are used to make tea. Leaves are used fresh or dried in soups and sauces. Their flavor is similar to anise." No source gives exact times or doses for preparation. No other admissible source was reachable, so no disagreement on scope or edibility can be reported.

records.name_note: NC State's rendered Common Name(s) list for Rumex scutatus is alphabetized (Buckler Leaved Sorrel first) and includes French Sorrel, and its description calls the plant French Sorrel. The RHS page for the same binomial shows French sorrel directly under its Rumex scutatus heading and lists "buckler-shaped sorrel, garden sorrel" as other common names. Sources agree on French Sorrel.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for Rumex scutatus has no Poison block, so it gives no severity rating, symptom list, toxic principle or poison-part list. Its Problems field lists Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs and Problem for Horses, and its Tags read #problem for horses, #problem for dogs, #problem for cats, #culinary, #groundcover, #creeping, #clumping, #mat forming, #edible leaves, #contact dermatitis, #microgreens. Its Plant Type field lists Annual, Edible, Herb. Its Uses (Ethnobotany) line reads "Used in salads, soups, and sauces. Tastes tart from its oxalic acid content, with a hint of lemon. Later in the season, it can be bitter." Its Edibility field reads "Leaves are used in salads and cooking." RHS's Rumex scutatus page says "the plant is usually grown for its edible leaves which can be cut for salads", and its Potentially harmful field reads in full: "Harmful if eaten in large amounts. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling Pets: Harmful if eaten in large amounts - for further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants". The RHS pet statement names no animal, so it is not used to support the cat/dog flag; toxic_to_pets true rests on NC State's cat- and dog-scoped Problems values and tags. Edibility is conditional: the leaves are the part named as eaten (NC State: salads and cooking; RHS: cut for salads), and RHS warns the plant is harmful if eaten in large amounts. No admissible source states what amount is harmful, a symptom list, or an oxalate threshold for people or pets.
unknowns: No poison section on NC State; toxic_to_pets=true rests on NC State's Problems field values (Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses) and the matching #problem-for tags only, with no symptoms, severity or poison part stated by any admissible source.

RHS says 'Pets: Harmful if eaten in large amounts' without naming an animal; not used for toxic_to_pets. RHS also says 'Harmful if eaten in large amounts. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling', while NC State ('Leaves are used in salads and cooking.') and RHS ('the plant is usually grown for its edible leaves which can be cut for salads') both describe the leaves as edible; NC State adds 'Later in the season, it can be bitter.'
Oxalate: NC State says the taste comes from oxalic acid content; no source gives a pet or human toxicity threshold.
NC State is internally inconsistent: Life Cycle says Perennial and the description says herbaceous perennial, but its Plant Type field lists Annual, Edible, Herb. RHS says Herbaceous Perennial.
Size sources differ: NC State Height 18-24 in and Width 16-36 in is used; RHS Max Height 0.1-0.5 m (3.9-19.7 in) and Max Spread 1-1.5 m (39.4-59.1 in) differ, especially in spread.
soil_ph_min/max null: NC State lists Acid, Neutral and Alkaline bands (open-ended) and RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral.

water_regime null: NC State's Moist drainage tag and RHS 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained' are soil descriptions, not watering statements; no admissible watering instruction was found. soil_drainage moderate comes from NC State's Good Drainage + Moist pair; RHS 'moist but well-drained' agrees.
soil_base garden_bed is a classification from NC State's in-ground cultural text (average, medium, well-drained soil); NC State also lists Container as a landscape location.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State lists Full sun and Partial Shade (2-6 hours direct sun) and RHS lists Full sun, Partial shade; mapped to full_sun and part_shade. direct_sun_hours_max left null (NC State's hour figures are the site legend for category tags).
attracts_pollinators null: NC State has no Attracts field; its Wildlife Value reads 'Food plant for caterpillars and' (truncated on the page), and RHS carries no pollinator tag in the fetched page.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames it as a houseplant. NC State's Plant Type field lists Annual, Edible and Herb, with no Houseplant value, it gives USDA zones 4a-9b, and its Landscape Location field lists Container and Small Space; RHS gives it hardiness H6.
No admissible source states temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, fertilizing, or chill damage figures; RHS H6 and NC State zones 4-9 are survival ratings, not damage onset.

records.name_note: Both admissible sources have a dedicated page for Satureja hortensis. RHS leads with 'summer savory' (page title 'Satureja hortensis | summer savory'). NC State's H1 is the botanical name and its Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Cimbru, Savory, Summer Savory), but its prose description opens 'Summer Savory is an edible, annual flowering herb'. Summer Savory was therefore chosen over "Cimbru" and the generic "Savory". This is the annual species and must stay distinct from Satureja montana (winter savory): NC State's S. hortensis page says "Summer Savory is grown as an annual, unlike its cousin, Winter Savory, which is grown as a perennial and tends to have a more bitter flavor.", and NC State's own Satureja montana page describes Winter Savory as "an edible, perennial flowering herb". No annual/perennial facts are merged.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for Satureja hortensis has no poison section. Its Tags line reads, in full: "#non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #companion plant #edible leaves #deer resistant #culinary #bushy #herbaceous perennial #herb #edible flowers". The non-toxic tags are NC State Tags (cats, horses, dogs), not a human poison rating; no admissible source gives a human poison rating, symptom list or handling warning. NC State's Plant Type field lists Edible, Herb, Herbaceous Perennial. NC State's Edibility field says: "Leaves, raw or cooked, can be used as flavoring. Aromatic and slightly peppery, it can be a garnish for salad or steeped for tea. Flowers are edible." No preparation time or condition is stated. The tag line includes #herbaceous perennial although NC State's Life Cycle is Annual (see unknowns). RHS (the only other admissible source with a page for this taxon) has no toxicity statement; it lists the plant under 'Herbs - Culinary'.
unknowns: No MoBot, Clemson, UF/IFAS, Penn State, UMD or UGA page dedicated to Satureja hortensis was found; only NC State and RHS have dedicated pages, so most fields rest on those two.

NC State is internally inconsistent on life cycle: Life Cycle is Annual and the description says annual, but its Plant Type field and a tag say Herbaceous Perennial. The annual reading is used (RHS's description says 'A bushy annual plant', though its type tags list Annual and Biennial).

is_houseplant false: no admissible source addresses indoor culture. NC State's Plant Type field lists Edible, Herb and Herbaceous Perennial, with no Houseplant value, and its Landscape Location lists Hanging Baskets and Small Space; RHS's suggested locations are outdoor garden types.
toxic_to_pets=false rests only on NC State's non-toxic-for-cats and non-toxic-for-dogs tags; no admissible source gives a human poison rating or a symptom list.

soil_drainage left null: NC State gives only a bare Good Drainage and RHS only a bare Well-drained, which is ambiguous on the fast/moderate scale. NC State's description also says both 'plenty of moisture' and 'does not do well in damp soil'.

water_regime and all watering/dry-down fields left null: NC State's prose is mixed (plenty of moisture vs not damp soil) and its drought/dry-soil resistance is a tolerance trait, not a watering instruction.
soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State gives only the open-ended Alkaline (>8.0) band and RHS says Alkaline or Neutral, so no ceiling or floor is set.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: the only hour figure is NC State's site-wide Light legend, not species prose. RHS also lists East-, South- or West-facing aspect, not used.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for Anthriscus cerefolium carries no Poison block, so there is no human-scoped severity rating or poison-part list to report. Its Tags line reads: "#edible garden #non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #partial shade tolerant #edible leaves #edible flowers #white flowers #biennial #showy leaves #early childhood #annual #herb garden #child #children #preschool #early care #easy edibles #edible", which includes the separate tags non-toxic for cats and non-toxic for dogs (the only cat/dog-scoped statement found). NC State's Plant Type field lists Annual, Edible, Herb. Its Edibility field reads: "Leaves common, but flowers and seeds as well; Use leaves in salads, soups, sauces, teas, and butters. Leaves can be harvested throughout the summer and fall." No admissible source gives a handling warning. No other admissible source addresses toxicity to pets, so the non-toxic reading rests on NC State's tags alone.

is_houseplant false: no admissible source frames chervil as a houseplant. soil_base left null: NC State says to sow seeds in the ground or in pots and RHS describes both in-ground and container culture (peat-free multi-purpose compost for containers), so garden_bed versus standard_potting is not settled by an admissible source.
soil_ph_max left null: NC State gives only the closed band Neutral (6.0-8.0) and no RHS pH field was available to check the ceiling against, so only the 6.0 floor is set.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade; its prose says partial to full sun; RHS recommends light shade, saying hot sun can cause premature flowering (bolting). Full sun is kept because NC State's structured field lists it; RHS's guidance is a caution about hot sun, not an exclusion.
direct_sun_hours_max left null: no species-specific hour figure outside NC State's generic light-category legend.

water_regime keep_moist is from RHS's chervil guide ('Aim to keep the soil/ compost consistently moist but not waterlogged'); RHS adds that regular watering delays bolting in hot, dry weather. NC State's Soil Drainage field lists Good Drainage and Moist, but its Resistance To Challenges field also lists Drought and Dry Soil (a tolerance trait, not a watering cadence). soil_drainage is moderate from NC State's Good Drainage + Moist pair and its 'moist well-drained soils' prose. No source gives a day interval or dry-down target, so those stay null.

Edibility: NC State covers leaves, flowers and seeds (Edibility field), and lists Leaf Value, Flower Value and Fruit Value To Gardener as Edible. RHS and UMD describe leaf use only. No admissible source on this page warns of toxic lookalikes, and none was added. NC State also lists 'Has been used medicinally in the past' under Uses (Ethnobotany).
toxic_to_pets false rests on NC State's non-toxic for cats / non-toxic for dogs tags only. NC State has no Poison block for this plant.

Temperature, humidity, light (foot-candle), fertilizer and chill-damage figures are not stated by any admissible source read; NC State's 'Humidity' under Resistance To Challenges is a tolerance trait, not a humidity need.

Size: NC State Dimensions give Height 1 ft 0 in - 2 ft 0 in (12-24 in) and Width 1 ft 0 in - 1 ft 6 in (12-18 in). RHS gives stems 30-60 cm (1-2 ft) tall, and UMD says up to 2 feet in height, both consistent with the NC State height.
